name: Oculinum

card.summary: Oculinum was the original name of botulinum toxin type A as developed by Alan Scott for eye-muscle disorders, the product that became Botox, whose wrinkle-smoothing effect later made it a cosmetic mainstay.
card.aka: original name of Botox; botulinum toxin A
card.note: Botulinum toxin is a prescription drug administered by clinicians.

quick.overview:
Oculinum was the first brand name of botulinum toxin A, developed by ophthalmologist Alan Scott to treat strabismus and eyelid spasm. Allergan acquired its maker and renamed it Botox.

The appearance link is the later cosmetic use: the same muscle-relaxing action smooths frown lines, which led to FDA approval for glabellar lines in 2002.
quick.how: Historically Oculinum was injected into eye muscles under guidance to relax them. Today's cosmetic equivalent is administered by clinicians in small injections into facial muscles, with effects wearing off over months.
quick.risks: Studies of Oculinum for facial spasm reported transient eyelid droop, double vision and altered expression, with no systemic effects in that series [1]. It is a prescription medicine given by trained clinicians.

lead: Oculinum was the name Alan Scott gave to botulinum toxin type A when he developed it for eye-muscle disorders in San Francisco; the name means roughly 'eye aligner' [2]. He injected the first strabismus patients in 1977 and reported clinical use in 1980 [2].

In 1986 Oculinum Inc. could not obtain liability insurance and supply paused; in 1989 the FDA approved it for strabismus and blepharospasm, and Allergan soon acquired the company and used the Botox trademark [2]. Reports in 1991 and 1992 on cosmetic use for frown lines led to FDA approval of Botox Cosmetic for glabellar lines in 2002 [2].

This history matters for appearance because the cosmetic neurotoxin used to smooth wrinkles grew directly out of an ophthalmic treatment. PubMed carries a review of Botox's early development history [3].

chain: Overactive muscles stop creasing the skin
angle.text: Oculinum is the historical name of the toxin whose later cosmetic version, Botox, relaxes facial muscles to soften expression lines. Its original use was treating strabismus and eyelid spasm.

paras: Scott and colleagues first tested botulinum toxin in monkey extraocular muscles, where tiny amounts paralysed the target muscle for a long period [2]. After 1977 patient work, he named it Oculinum in 1980 and trained ophthalmologists in EMG-guided injection [2].
Oculinum Inc. paused supply in 1986 over insurance; the 1989 FDA approval covered adult strabismus and blepharospasm, after which Allergan acquired the company [2].

A 1991 review described use in strabismus (especially postoperative overcorrection, small deviations and acute sixth nerve palsy), blepharospasm and hemifacial spasm, with temporary relief [4]. A series of 105 patients with facial spasm saw control of spasm, effects lasting three to four months [1].
The Carruthers cosmetic study was reported in 1991, with 16 of 17 followed-up patients improving, and published in 1992; Botox Cosmetic was approved for glabellar lines in 2002 [2].

Studies from the 1980s evaluated Oculinum for facial spasm [1], strabismus [5][6] and in ophthalmology more broadly [4]. The 105-patient facial-spasm series reported transient ptosis in 7, diplopia in 2 and altered expression in 11, without systemic effects [1].

timeline.event: Scott reports clinical utility and names the drug Oculinum [2].
FDA approves for strabismus and blepharospasm; Allergan acquires maker [2].
FDA approves Botox Cosmetic for glabellar lines [2].
